what_its_for: Penicillamine is used to treat Wilson's disease (a condition where too much copper builds up in your body), severe rheumatoid arthritis when other treatments have not worked, and cystinuria (a kidney stone condition caused by too much cystine in the urine). It works by binding to certain metals and substances in your body and helping your body remove them.
how_to_take: Take penicillamine by mouth on an empty stomach, at least 1 hour before meals or 2 hours after meals, and at least 1 hour away from any other medicines, food, or milk. Swallow the capsule or tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you are taking it for Wilson's disease or cystinuria, drink plenty of water throughout the day, especially at night. Always take it exactly as your doctor told you.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, weight, and how well your body responds to the medicine. Your doctor will usually start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time. For adults, doses typically range from 250 mg to 1,500 mg per day, taken in divided doses. For children, the dose is based on body weight. Never change your dose or stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still at least 1 to 2 hours before your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store penicillamine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in the original container, away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking iron supplements, antacids, or other mineral supplements within 2 hours of taking penicillamine, as they can block how well the medicine works. Avoid taking penicillamine with food or milk. Do not receive certain vaccines without talking to your doctor first. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine, as it may harm an unborn baby — talk to your doctor about birth control. Limit sun exposure, as penicillamine may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you notice: fever, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; skin rash, hives, or blistering; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; muscle weakness or difficulty swallowing or breathing; blood in your urine or changes in how much urine you make; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); double vision or drooping eyelids; or any new or worsening symptoms. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Penicillamine works slowly. For rheumatoid arthritis, it may take 2 to 3 months before you notice improvement in your joint pain and swelling, and sometimes up to 6 months for the full effect. For Wilson's disease and cystinuria, your doctor will monitor lab tests to check that the medicine is working. Do not stop taking it just because you do not feel immediate results — it takes time.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Penicillamine can cause serious birth defects and should generally not be used during pregnancy unless your doctor decides the benefit outweighs the risk (such as in Wilson's disease). Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects and should be monitored closely. Children: Dosing is based on body weight and must be determined by a doctor. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need adjustment. Penicillin allergy: Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin, although cross-allergy is rare, your doctor needs to know.
